gist: Atwood argues that the adepts and Theurgists reached the captive inner Light by patient, rational, experiential inquiry, in which natural reason is only an 'iron key' and the real agent is a freed spiritual Intellect, the 'true Separator', called also Wisdom, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture. The Hermetic Separation is identified with the death-and-resurrection ordeals of the Mysteries, and the chunk closes with Anaxagoras on Intellect as the unmingled power that separates all things.

notes.point: Physicians freed this Light to cure bodily ills; the Theurgic Art purified and informed the Mind, nearest to Christ's doctrine of regeneration: baptismal purification, gradual subjugation of passions to reason, then conversion of the whole hypostasis through faith into substant light within.

To find this Reason the ancients questioned Nature rationally, not destructively like modern chemistry; admitted from within as lawful guests, they sought not phenomena but worthiness of nature's own light.
Theurgists consulted the divine intellect only on purification, liberation, salvation of life and discovery of truth.

Every beginner first wanders among chimeras. Rightly begun, inquiry traces vital causes to Deity, whence adepts worked supernatural perfection below; their sole aim was the Central Light and Wisdom, until the hidden Divinity became manifest in experience.
Examine patiently, infer from experience, follow God's Rule; help nature beyond her common course; the Mercury of the Wise comes only by ingenuity and industry.
Crollius: holy assiduity of preparations, contemplation, handiwork and infused grace yield more than nature promises. Van Helmont: the Tree of Life is laborious intellectual research.
Basil Valentine: find nature's concealed first foundation with your own eyes and hand, or build on sand; adepts demand proof by experience, not words.
All adepts (Lully, Michael Maier, others) agree the way to Wisdom is patience and rational inquiry into intimate causes.
Basil: the second part is celestial, grasped by spiritual reason: nature perfected by its own resolution, destruction and compaction handled to separate pure from impure.

No graft from this life enters the divine foundation. Natural reason is dull and inoperative here, only an iron key on the threshold; once it brings the spiritual intellect into self-knowledge, that intellect returns upon the outer life and transforms it by the fiery essence of its new Law.

This vital perscrutinator (Eirenaeus' 'internal fire of the sulfur of thy water') operates the whole change; only its holders pass the narrow gate to the Magistery of life, as in the Mysteries. It is the flower of intellect, triply imprisoned in the body; only a lover of Wisdom can free it.

Eirenaeus: our fire, sulfur and seed of gold, is imprisoned in the hard body; our water frees it by rotting the body (glossed: ethereal body); after separation of elements it appears in the Third Menstrual, hidden from those ignorant of the first two.

Practice: join the first water to the body in just pondus, seal until the infant forms, govern fire so external heat cherishes internal, await signs (pores opened, tincture of Sol partly extracted). Mind the internal Fire over the Athanor's; Aries, Saturn, Mercury the internal, Doves of Diana the signal.
Parallel: the Sybil sends Aeneas for the Golden Bough, sought upward; it yields to the fated, not to force.

Orpheus' Cave of Mercury is, by Hermetic interpretation, Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life; the prudent seeker, allied to what he seeks, carries off the mineral radix. Without right mind and the predestined order of operation, the power stays hidden in an uncongenial soul.
Fire loves fire, to assimilate gold, not make it: throw the true gold-body (not a brazen ferment) into a bottomless Mercury, whose center it finds only by finding its own.

The art of Oedipus subdues the Sphinx: the Ethereal Spirit abandons phantasy and yields understanding to the trained inquirer. Synesius: Intellect purifies phantastic Spirit and extends it to Divinity; natural Intellect cannot.

Language fails to convey the adepts' claim that a freed will refines its own vehicle into universal intelligence, above all to an age without experimental knowledge of causality; Atwood will attempt it.

Paracelsus' Separation, 'the greatest miracle in philosophy', is identical with the Mysteries' death of natural life: suffering, dread, dissolution, corruption, resurrection of pure Ether into Light. It is the Art's primary object.

Paracelsus: the creature has free power in Separation; free will is friend or foe; the sequestatrix gives form and essence (Atwood: this is Intellect, Hermes' perscrutinating Intellect). Tablet: separate subtle from gross gently. Asclepius: man can effect the Causal Nature.
notes.voice: QUOTED: Paracelsus; Hermes (glossed and endorsed by Atwood)

notes.point: Hence decomposition is not mechanical: Mind is the true Separator and regimen, admitting no foreign admixture; nothing is found unless the matter is decomposed and the whole introversion passed. The great Master: the matter is One only Thing.
Folly, phantasy, passion and Reason are modes of the One Thing; as phantasy turns all to folly, Reason ascendant ferments all into its Light, as the Head Stone writers intimate.

Ordinary reason and the standard of faith are images of the higher Reason, called Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture. It is Light; as the sun sublimes matter, the Intellectual sun rejects false forms, triturates foreign tincture, and infuses itself into the passified Spirit.

Anaxagoras (via Simplicius, Taylor): Intellect is infinite, unmingled, purest, all-knowing, ruling soul; it separated dense from rare, hot from cold, lucid from dark, dry from moist; it alone is singular, and all Intellect is alike.

method.veiled: To find this Light, and to free it from captivity
method.plain: What is sought is a Light held captive, to be found and freed: by physicians for bodily cure, by the Theurgic Art for purifying and informing the Mind.
method.basis: III.1 ¶11 states both uses directly.

method.veiled: an effectual baptismal purification
method.plain: A first purification that 'prepared the way' for what followed; its nature is not specified.
method.basis: III.1 ¶11: 'by an effectual baptismal purification, they also prepared the way'.

method.veiled: a gradual subjugation of the passions and adaptation of the subordinate powers to reason
method.plain: Step by step the passions are mastered and the lower faculties brought under reason.

method.veiled: the whole hypostasis was converted finally through faith into the identity of substant light within
method.plain: Finally the whole being is turned, through faith, into identity with the inner light.
method.basis: III.1 ¶11, last step of the stated sequence; 'hypostasis' read as the whole subject because the conversion is of 'the whole'; the chunk does not define the word.

method.veiled: put the question to Nature rationally
method.plain: Inquire of nature by reason, not by destroying her as modern chemistry does.
method.basis: III.1 ¶12: 'not rudely indeed, or, as is with modern chemistry the fashion, to demolish her edifices'.

method.veiled: they knocked as was bid them, and the doors being opened from within
method.plain: Entry to nature's inner chamber is granted from inside to those who ask as directed; it is not forced.
method.basis: III.1 ¶12 contrasts this with demolishing nature and calls them 'lawful guests'; cf. ¶13 'narrow gate' and 'passport'.

method.veiled: not much engaged in noting phenomena, or looking about for facts to furnish private judgment
method.plain: Once admitted, the inquirer does not gather phenomena but seeks to become worthy of nature's own light; 'they were not content with first phenomena'.

method.veiled: sphered in the magian circle of her own light
method.plain: Nature, once entered, is found exalted above the inquirers in her own light, which they seek to become worthy to know.
method.basis: III.1 ¶12: 'that they might approach nearer and become worthy of the knowledge and familiarity of that light'.

method.veiled: they consulted it about things which pertain to purification, liberation, as Iamblicus tells us, and the salvation of life
method.plain: The divine intellect is consulted only about purification, liberation and salvation, never trifles.

method.veiled: he wanders awhile in the region of chimeras
method.plain: Every beginner makes many, often erroneous inquiries before reaching experimental knowledge.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'the inquiries which he makes before attaining to experimental knowledge are many, and often erroneous'.

method.veiled: having set the chain of vital causes in action, succeeded in tracing them to their last efficient link in Deity
method.plain: Adepts set a series of vital causes working and followed it to its source in God, whence, under the divine will, they worked supernatural effects 'in things below'.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'whence surveying, they were enabled, under the divine will, to work such perfection in things below'.

method.veiled: For the Central Light and Wisdom was all their aim
method.plain: The goal is the Central Light and Wisdom, pursued 'until the hidden Divinity was moved into experience and made manifest in effect and power'.

method.veiled: Lay the line to thy thoughts and examine all patiently, and infer from experience
method.plain: Regulate one's thinking, examine patiently and draw conclusions from experience, guided by 'that Rule which God hath given thee'.

method.veiled: you must help her, that she may exceed her common course, or all is to no purpose
method.plain: Nature alone does not yield the result and must not be asked for more than her strength; the operator must assist her beyond her ordinary course.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'Seek not for that in nature which is an effect beyond her strength'.

method.veiled: the Mercury of the Wise comes not but by help of ingenuity and industry
method.plain: The Mercury of the Wise is not found ready-made; it is obtained only by the operator's skill and labor. What it is, the chunk does not say.

method.veiled: a holy assiduity of preparations, joining thereto diligent contemplation of natural causes
method.plain: The operator needs devout, persistent preparation, contemplation of causes, manual experience, and infused grace.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'shall refuse no pains or difficulties to get experience by the industry of his handy work, he shall, if the grace of the most high be infused into him'.

method.veiled: the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research
method.plain: The goal is reached by hard labor and intellectual research.

method.veiled: Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed
method.plain: Nature hides a first foundation that must be found by direct experience ('with thine own eyes and hand'); without it, reasoning is 'built upon sand'.

method.veiled: rather exact documents proved by experience, in which we are bounden to have faith
method.plain: Adepts accept only what experience proves, not mere words.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'Let not any one imagine either that we can be satisfied with mere words'.

method.veiled: how nature may be helped and perfected by resolution of itself, and how the destruction and compaction are to be handled
method.plain: Nature is perfected by dissolving into itself; a destroying and a consolidating phase are managed so that the pure is separated from the impure. Grasped only by spiritual reason.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'whereby under a just title, without sophistical deceits, the pure may be separated from the impure'; 'to be understood with spiritual reason'.

method.veiled: it is no graft from this life that enters into the divine foundation, nor any arbitrary instinct
method.plain: Nothing grafted on from ordinary life, and no arbitrary impulse, enters the divine foundation.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13; parallels ¶21 'no foreign admixture is allowed to enter'. 'Graft' read as something added from outside.

method.veiled: as it were an iron key, intended to unlock the golden treasury of light within
method.plain: Natural reason is necessary but only a threshold tool: it opens access to the inner light and to the spiritual intellect, but does not itself do the work.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: natural reason 'is dull here comparatively, and inoperative, and stands in the Philosophic Work, albeit necessary, as a mere circumstantial aid on the threshold'.

method.veiled: this latter, returning with power upon the life without, proceeds to analyze and revolutionize
method.plain: Once brought into self-knowledge, the spiritual intellect turns outward on the outer life and transforms it, 'proving all... chemically by the fiery essence of its newly conceived Law'.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: natural reason 'helped to introduce the spiritual intellect into self-knowledge'.

method.veiled: the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water
method.plain: Eirenaeus' name for the 'vital perscrutinator' that 'operates the whole change'; in context, the self-knowing spiritual intellect just described.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13 states the naming and that it 'operates the whole change'. Identifying it with the spiritual intellect rests on 'this' referring back to the preceding sentence, and on ¶20-21 where Intellect is the separating agent.

method.veiled: they only who have obtained this passport can attain to the Magistery of life
method.plain: Only those in whom this inner agent is awakened can complete the work; this bars intruders, like the narrow gate of the Mysteries.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'they only, literally speaking, can enter in through the narrow gate, as in the Mysteries'.

method.veiled: the discovery is difficult, and reputed tedious by many who have spared no labor either of body or mind in the research
method.plain: The discovery is hard and slow even for those who labor at it, because what is sought is hidden far within.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'it is far off, gotten in the penetralia'.

method.veiled: the flower of human intellect, triply imprisoned in the dark body’s hold
method.plain: What is sought is the highest part of human intellect, locked deep in the body; the philosopher's business is to free it. 'Triply' is not explained.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'This it is the business of the philosopher to open and set free'.

method.veiled: he must be a lover of Wisdom who can set her free
method.plain: Only a true lover of Wisdom can free what is imprisoned; this requirement is itself the safeguard.
method.basis: III.1 ¶13: 'this is the security'.

method.veiled: Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold
method.plain: The active fire of the work, also called 'the seed of gold', is imprisoned in the hard dry body and set loose by 'our water'.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14. Compare ¶13 'the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water'.

method.veiled: by the mediation of our water it is set loose, by rotting the moles of the body (i.e., of the ethereal body)
method.plain: A 'water' frees the fire by putrefying the masses of the body that detain it; a parenthetical gloss says this is the ethereal body. What 'our water' is, is not stated.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14. 'Moles' read as masses from 'under which it is detained'. The glosses '(i.e., of the ethereal body)' and '(of the same body)' sit inside the quotation and are unmarked; see ambiguities.

method.veiled: it appears visibly in our Third Menstrual
method.plain: After the body's elements separate, the freed fire becomes visible at a third stage or medium, reachable only through knowledge of the first two.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14: 'he that knows not our two first menstruals is altogether shut out from attaining to the sight of this Third and last'. 'Menstrual' is not defined.

method.veiled: it requires a profound meditation
method.plain: Finding the means to free the fire is no light work; it needs deep meditation.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14: 'the means to discover this is not a light work'.

method.veiled: to prepare the first water, and to join it to the body in a just pondus
method.plain: Prepare the first water and join it to the body in the right proportion.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14. 'Pondus' read as weight/proportion; the text does not gloss it.

method.veiled: to shut it up in its vessel philosophically, until the infant be formed
method.plain: Seal the compound in its vessel and leave it until something new (the 'infant') forms. What vessel and infant stand for is not stated.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14 only.

method.veiled: to govern his fire dexterously, so as to cherish internal heat with external
method.plain: The chief skill: regulate the applied heat so that outer heat sustains the inner heat.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14 calls this 'what is greater than all'.

method.veiled: can wait with patience till he sees signs
method.plain: The operator waits patiently for visible signs before proceeding.

method.veiled: opened the pores and extracted partly the tincture of Sol
method.plain: The first sign: the first water opens the body and partly draws out its 'tincture of Sol', i.e. the gold-principle the ancients name Sol and Tincture.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14 'he shall perceive the first water will work on the body till...'; ¶21 lists 'Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture' among names of the Reason/Intellect.

method.veiled: be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire
method.plain: The furnace's outer fire matters less than the internal Fire.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14; consistent with ¶13, where the internal fire 'operates the whole change'. Speaker uncertain; see ambiguities.

method.veiled: Seek it in the house of Aries, and draw it from the depths of Saturn
method.plain: Directions for where to find the internal Fire; the chunk gives no key to Aries or Saturn.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14: 'it' follows 'your internal Fire'. See ambiguities.

method.veiled: let Mercury be the internal, and your signal the Doves of Diana
method.plain: Mercury is to be 'the internal', and the 'Doves of Diana' are a signal to watch for; neither is explained here.
method.basis: III.1 ¶14 only; 'signal' follows the earlier 'wait with patience till he sees signs'.

method.veiled: well directing him how to look from beneath upwards, and take it in hand
method.plain: As with the Golden Bough, the seeker searches upward through obscurity and takes the thing in hand; it yields freely only to one the fates call, never to force.
method.basis: III.1 ¶15 'On some such errand' links it to the preceding search; ¶16 Latin (our translation) 'Si te fate vocant; aliter, non viribus ullis Vincere'.

method.veiled: the Cave of Mercury, which, according to the Hermetic interpretation, is Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life
method.plain: The 'cave' where the goods lie is the most hidden vapor of life.

method.veiled: the mineral radix and true mater of the Hermetic Art
method.plain: What the rightly disposed seeker carries out of the Cave of Mercury is the root and true matter of the Art.

method.veiled: let him enter with a prudent motive, well understanding and allied to what he seeks
method.plain: The seeker needs a prudent motive, real understanding, and affinity with what he seeks.

method.veiled: the power will remain hidden, despite of every effort, in a pusillanimous uncongenial soul
method.plain: Without a right mind and observance of 'the predestined conditions and the order of operation', no effort succeeds; a faint-hearted, unsuited soul cannot bring the power out.
method.basis: III.1 ¶19: 'if he have not a right mind, and unless the predestined conditions and the order of operation be observed, all will be in vain'.

method.veiled: Fire loves fire, say they, not to make gold, but to assimilate it
method.plain: The active fire does not manufacture gold; it assimilates what it acts on to itself.
method.basis: III.1 ¶19 gives 'assimilate'; 'to itself' rests on ¶21: Reason 'would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence' and works by 'assimilating the whole inferior life'.

method.veiled: Take, therefore, that body which is gold (not a brazen ferment), and throw it into Mercury
method.plain: Put the true gold-body, not a base ferment, into a 'bottomless' Mercury. What the gold-body and Mercury refer to is not stated.
method.basis: III.1 ¶19 only; on the 'bottomless' Mercury see ambiguities.

method.veiled: This is the art of Oedipus which, well conducted with the Sphinx, ends in her subjugation
method.plain: The work subdues the Ethereal Spirit: she gives up her phantasy and yields clear understanding to the properly trained investigator.
method.basis: III.1 ¶20: 'in other words, the Ethereal Spirit abandons her phantasy, and yields the clear light of understanding'.

method.veiled: having been duly educated and singled out, knows how and wherewith to investigate her peculiar essence
method.plain: The investigator must be properly trained, chosen, and know both the method and the means of examining the Spirit's own essence.

method.veiled: Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit
method.plain: Intellect purifies the image-making spirit, attenuating it 'in an occult and ineffable manner' and extending it to Divinity. Natural intellect cannot.
method.basis: III.1 ¶20: 'But the natural Intellect cannot do this... neither is its essence so acutely penetrative as to operate the change required'.

method.veiled: the efficient force of an individual freed will upon the vehicle of its motive cause
method.plain: A freed individual will acts on its own vehicle, 'separating, refining, and transmuting it from an impure, dull consistency to the clear light of universal intelligence'.
method.basis: III.1 ¶20, presented as the adepts' assertion.

method.veiled: This Separation is indeed the primary object of the Art
method.plain: Separation, which Paracelsus calls 'the greatest miracle in philosophy', is the Art's main aim, and is the same as the separation in the Mysteries during 'the decomposition and death of the natural life'.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'appears to be identical with that which is described as taking place in the Mysteries'.

method.veiled: suffering, succedent dread, dissolution, and corruption, to the final resurrection of the pure Ether into Light
method.plain: Separation runs: suffering, then dread, dissolution, corruption, and finally the rising of the purified Ether as Light.

method.veiled: there is a free power in the creature to its mutual affection and destruction
method.plain: Separation is not God's work alone; the creature has a free power in it, and free will can help or hinder the work.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'if it were divinely done by God alone, it would be to no purpose to study after it'; 'The free will... is either friend or foe in our works'.

method.veiled: that is the sequestatrix, which gives to every thing its form and essence
method.plain: The separating power that gives things form and essence; Atwood identifies it as Intellect.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'which is the part especial of Intellect, that same perscrutinating Intellect which Hermes speaks of'.

method.veiled: Thou shalt separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently, with much sagacity
method.plain: Separate subtle from gross, gently and wisely; Atwood reads this as the work of Intellect/Mind.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21, n22; 'according to the literal wording of the Table, we observe Mind to be the true Separator'.

method.veiled: it will ascend from earth to heaven, and again descend from heaven to earth, and will receive the strength of the Inferiors and of the Superiors
method.plain: The separated subtle part rises and returns, gaining power from above and below: 'the strong fortitude of all fortitudes'. Not further glossed.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: follows the separation command in the Tablet citation.

method.veiled: man should be able not only to find the Causal Nature but to effect it
method.plain: Man can not only discover the causal nature of things but bring it about.

method.veiled: we observe Mind to be the true Separator, the efficient as well as the regimen of the work
method.plain: Mind both performs and governs the work; the 'decomponency of life' is not mechanical or ordinary dissolution.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'Nor ought we... to understand this decomponency of life in a mechanical sense'.

method.veiled: no foreign admixture is allowed to enter
method.plain: Nothing foreign may be added to the work.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21 ('as before shown'); cf. ¶13 'it is no graft from this life that enters into the divine foundation'.

method.veiled: not corporally or imprudently sought after, but is through patience and Wisdom to be discovered according to their causes and their occult operation
method.plain: The ancients' elements are known not by physical handling but through patience and Wisdom, by their causes and hidden operation.

method.veiled: nothing is discovered except the matte be decomposed, and because it is not perfected unless the whole introversion is passed through
method.plain: Nothing is found until the matter is decomposed, and nothing perfected until a complete turning-inward has run its course.

method.veiled: the whole matter I know to be One only Thing
method.plain: The matter of the work is one single thing, of which folly, phantasy, passion and Reason are modes.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21, n24; next sentence: 'folly, and phantasy, and passion are modes of being of the One Thing, and Reason is another'.
method.voice: QUOTED: the great Master (Tract. Aur., n24) (endorsed)

method.veiled: this Reason gaining the ascendancy, would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence and traction of her own Light
method.plain: When Reason dominates the One Thing, it converts the rest into its own Light as leaven does; if phantasy prevails, all turns to folly.

method.veiled: abundantly celebrating the virtues of their Head Stone
method.plain: The 'Head Stone' of Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber is linked by Atwood to Reason fermenting all into Light.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'This Lully intimates; and Arnold, and Bacon, and Geber...' directly follows the ferment sentence.

method.veiled: these things which the natural reason as an image enacts theoretically, this supernatural reason is said to do as an archetype essentially
method.plain: Ordinary reason's work (judging, governing passions, separating fact from falsehood) is an image of what the higher Reason does in substance; the former gives a glimpse of the latter.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'let him for a plea only regard the image of it in this life. What else is it but reason, that enables us to analyze and judge opinion, to govern our passions'.

method.veiled: so are we taught to conceive of the Intellectual sun
method.plain: The higher Reason/Intellect acts on the inner life as the sun on matter: purifying, subtilizing, subliming and converting.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'as the luminary of the sensible world purifies and subtilizes the gross parts of matter... so are we taught to conceive of the Intellectual sun'.

method.veiled: assimilating the whole inferior life by continual trituration of its foreign tincture
method.plain: Supernatural reason rejects false forms and elementary qualities acquired through generation, grinds away the foreign coloring of the lower life to assimilate it, and perfects deficient faculties by pouring itself into the passive Spirit.
method.basis: III.1 ¶21: 'separating and rejecting the false forms and elementary qualities which supervene through generation'; 'by pure infusion of Itself to the passified Spirit throughout'.

method.veiled: Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing; but is alone by itself
method.plain: Intellect rules and separates all things because it is itself unmixed; mingled, it would lose that dominion.
method.basis: III.1 ¶22: 'things mingled together would prevent it from having a similar dominion over things'; Atwood cites it (¶21) as confirming Intellect's 'efficient operation'.

method.veiled: separated the dense from the rare, the hot from the cold, the lucid from the dark, and the dry from the moist
method.plain: Intellect is the power that separates contraries.
method.basis: III.1 ¶22: 'this comprehending Intellect made things to be separated'.

terms.meaning: The captive inner principle freed by physicians for healing and by Theurgy for the Mind; the adepts' aim, with Wisdom; the Reason/Intellect is said to be Light.

equivalences.quote: For it is Light indeed, and an occult splendor of existence transcendentally pure

quotes.text: To find this Light, and to free it from captivity
For the Central Light and Wisdom was all their aim

terms.meaning: An art claiming power to purify and inform the Mind, beyond bodily healing; proceeds by baptismal purification, subjugation of passions to reason, conversion through faith into inner light; consults the divine intellect only on purification, liberation and salvation.

quotes.text: the Theurgic Art professed a power of purifying and informing the Mind much more beneficial and lasting than this pertaining to the mortal body

terms.meaning: The perfect doctrine preached by Jesus Christ and his apostles, which the Theurgic Art came nearest to fulfilling.

quotes.text: a fulfillment of the perfect doctrine of regeneration preached by Jesus Christ and his apostles

terms.meaning: The whole that is converted into the inner light; not defined in the chunk. n26 mentions a treatise 'on the Gnostic Hypostasis'.

quotes.text: the whole hypostasis was converted finally through faith into the identity of substant light within

terms.meaning: The adepts' aim with the Central Light; reached by patience and rational inquiry; the imprisoned thing only a lover of Wisdom can 'set her free'; one of the ancients' names for the higher Reason.

equivalences.with: Reason / Intellect / Gold / Sol / Sulfur / Tincture
equivalences.quote: it is of this the ancients speak, calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture

quotes.text: he must be a lover of Wisdom who can set her free
they all agree that the way to Wisdom is by patience and rational inquiry

terms.meaning: The higher Reason the ancients sought by questioning Nature; distinct from natural reason, its image; a mode of the One Thing that, ascendant, gathers all as a ferment into its own Light; works essentially as archetype.

equivalences.with: Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture
equivalences.quote: calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture

quotes.text: in order to discover this Reason, men had in former times the faith to put the question to Nature rationally
this Reason gaining the ascendancy, would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence and traction of her own Light

terms.meaning: Ordinary reason: necessary but dull and inoperative in the divine work, a threshold aid only; cannot purify the phantastic Spirit; image of the higher Reason; analyzes opinion, governs passions, separates fact from falsehood.

equivalences.quote: as it were an iron key, intended to unlock the golden treasury of light within

quotes.text: natural reason, even the most acute, is dull here comparatively, and inoperative
But the natural Intellect cannot do this, neither comprehending properly, or being conceived of the Spirit

terms.meaning: In Basil's words, the faculty by which the celestial second part of the work is understood: how nature is perfected by its own resolution and pure separated from impure. Not explicitly equated with the spiritual intellect.

quotes.text: to be understood with spiritual reason
cannot be perceived any other way than by the spiritual cognitation of man

terms.meaning: The higher intellect that natural reason helps bring into self-knowledge; it then acts with power on the outer life, analyzing and transforming it by the fiery essence of its new Law.

quotes.text: this latter, returning with power upon the life without, proceeds to analyze and revolutionize

terms.meaning: The searching inner agent that 'operates the whole change'; Eirenaeus' 'internal fire of the sulfur of thy water'; Atwood speaks of Hermes' 'perscrutinating Intellect' as the separating Intellect.

equivalences.with: internal fire of the sulfur of thy water
equivalences.quote: It is this vital perscrutinator, the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water, as Eirenaeus calls it

quotes.text: that same perscrutinating Intellect which Hermes speaks of

terms.meaning: The agent of Separation: purifies and extends the phantastic Spirit to Divinity, gives things form and essence, is the true Separator and regimen of the work; per Anaxagoras, infinite, unmingled, most pure, ruling and ordering all, separating contraries.

equivalences.quote: that is the sequestatrix, which gives to every thing its form and essence (20); which is the part especial of Intellect
we observe Mind to be the true Separator, the efficient as well as the regimen of the work
calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture

quotes.text: Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing
no one thing is singular by itself except Intellect

terms.meaning: The primary object of the Art and philosophy's greatest miracle; identical with the Mysteries' decomposition and death of natural life ending in pure Ether's resurrection into Light; effected by Mind/Intellect, not mechanically.

equivalences.quote: appears to be identical with that which is described as taking place in the Mysteries, when the great ordeals are passed through during the decomposition and death of the natural life

quotes.text: Separation is the greatest miracle in philosophy
This Separation is indeed the primary object of the Art

terms.meaning: What the Alchemists 'distil'; the pure Ether rises into Light at the end of Separation; the Ethereal Spirit (the Sphinx) yields up phantasy under right investigation; a gloss identifies Eirenaeus' imprisoning 'body' as the ethereal body.

equivalences.quote: by rotting the moles of the body (i.e., of the ethereal body)

quotes.text: But what say our Oedipus distillers of this Ether, the instructive Alchemists?
the final resurrection of the pure Ether into Light

terms.meaning: The image-making mode of the Spirit and of the One Thing; prevailing, it converts the inner life to folly; Intellect separates what is contrary to the purity of the phantastic Spirit.

quotes.text: as the phantasy, if suffered to prevail, will convert all to her own folly in the internal life
true purity of phantastic Spirit

terms.meaning: The art of investigating the Ethereal Spirit (the Sphinx) until she abandons phantasy and gives clear understanding.

equivalences.quote: ends in her subjugation; in other words, the Ethereal Spirit abandons her phantasy

quotes.text: This is the art of Oedipus which, well conducted with the Sphinx, ends in her subjugation

terms.meaning: The single matter of the work; folly, phantasy, passion and Reason are its modes.

quotes.text: the whole matter I know to be One only Thing
folly, and phantasy, and passion are modes of being of the One Thing, and Reason is another

terms.meaning: The Mercury of the Wise comes only by ingenuity and industry (Alchemists); the Cave of Mercury is, by Hermetic interpretation, Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life, source of the mineral radix (Atwood); the gold-body is thrown into a bottomless Mercury ('they'); 'let Mercury be the internal' (Eirenaeus).

equivalences.with: Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life
equivalences.quote: the Cave of Mercury, which, according to the Hermetic interpretation, is Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life

quotes.text: the Mercury of the Wise comes not but by help of ingenuity and industry
such a Mercury as is bottomless, or whose center it can never find, but by discovering its own

variants: true mater of the Hermetic Art
terms.meaning: What the rightly disposed seeker carries out of the Cave of Mercury: the root and true matter of the Art.

equivalences.with: true mater of the Hermetic Art
equivalences.quote: will be the mineral radix and true mater of the Hermetic Art

terms.meaning: The fire of the work, imprisoned in the hard dry body and set loose by our water; also one of the ancients' names for the higher Reason.

equivalences.quote: Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold, says Eirenaeus
for this is the seed of gold, involved in many links, and held prisoner

quotes.text: the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water

terms.meaning: The inner fire, more important than the furnace fire; external heat must cherish it.

quotes.text: be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire
so as to cherish internal heat with external

terms.meaning: The medium that frees the imprisoned fire by rotting the body; the first water, prepared and joined to the body, opens its pores and partly extracts the tincture of Sol. The chunk does not say whether it is one of the menstruals.

quotes.text: by the mediation of our water it is set loose
the first water will work on the body till it hath opened the pores

terms.meaning: A series of three; the freed fire appears visibly in the Third, which cannot be reached without knowing the first two. Not otherwise defined.

quotes.text: it appears visibly in our Third Menstrual
he that knows not our two first menstruals is altogether shut out from attaining to the sight of this Third and last

terms.meaning: The measure in which the first water is joined to the body; not defined in the text.

quotes.text: to join it to the body in a just pondus

terms.meaning: The furnace, whose fire matters less than the internal Fire.

quotes.text: be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire

terms.meaning: One of the ancients' names for the higher Reason; its tincture is partly extracted from the body by the first water.

equivalences.quote: calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture

quotes.text: extracted partly the tincture of Sol

terms.meaning: One of the ancients' names for the higher Reason; also the 'foreign tincture' of inferior life that supernatural reason grinds away.

quotes.text: assimilating the whole inferior life by continual trituration of its foreign tincture

terms.meaning: One of the ancients' names for the higher Reason; the body 'which is gold', as opposed to a brazen ferment, is thrown into Mercury; fire assimilates rather than makes it.

equivalences.quote: calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture

quotes.text: Take, therefore, that body which is gold (not a brazen ferment), and throw it into Mercury

terms.meaning: What converts a mass into its own nature: Reason gathers all up 'as a ferment'. A 'brazen ferment' is the wrong body to use.

quotes.text: would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence and traction of her own Light

terms.meaning: The goal attainable only by those holding the 'passport' of the awakened inner agent.

quotes.text: they only who have obtained this passport can attain to the Magistery of life

terms.meaning: The Hermetic operation, in which natural reason is only a threshold aid and Mind is Separator and regimen.

quotes.text: stands in the Philosophic Work, albeit necessary, as a mere circumstantial aid on the threshold of the divine inquiry

terms.meaning: What Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber celebrate; linked by Atwood to Reason gathering all into its Light.

quotes.text: abundantly celebrating the virtues of their Head Stone

terms.meaning: A complete process, which must be wholly passed through before the work is perfected.

quotes.text: it is not perfected unless the whole introversion is passed through

terms.meaning: The ancients' elements are known by their causes and occult operation, not corporally; elementary qualities supervening through generation are rejected by the Intellectual sun.

quotes.text: the knowledge of the elements of the ancient philosophers was not corporally or imprudently sought after

terms.meaning: The creature's free power in the work, 'either friend or foe'; a freed will acts efficiently on its own vehicle to refine it.

quotes.text: The free will flourisheth and is conversant in virtue, and is either friend or foe in our works

terms.meaning: That which, per the Asclepius, man can both find and effect.

quotes.text: man should be able not only to find the Causal Nature but to effect it

terms.meaning: Atwood's name for the doctrine of mind's magic action and the freed will acting on its vehicle, which she undertakes to 'substantialize without deforming'.

quotes.text: to substantialize without deforming this Intellectual Science

terms.meaning: In the Alchemists' counsel, the God-given rule for discerning right from wrong; Atwood later speaks of 'the Reason of our Rule' as the higher Reason glimpsed through the 'standard of our common faith'. The chunk does not explicitly link the two uses.

quotes.text: Take hold of that Rule which God hath given thee for direction, by which thou mayest discern the right from the wrong
the superior virtue of that which is the Reason of our Rule

terms.meaning: Its attainment is laborious and the fruit of intellectual research.

quotes.text: the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research

terms.meaning: The basis nature holds concealed, to be found by personal experience.

quotes.text: Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed

terms.meaning: Object of Aeneas' search, offered as parallel to the hidden thing sought; yields only to one the fates call.

quotes.text: he may discover and bring to her the Golden Bough

terms.meaning: Pertaining to the adepts' school, to nature's own sphere of light, and to mind's power acting in its own spheres.

quotes.text: No man enters the magian’s school
the magic action of mind in her own spheres

terms.meaning: Their ordeals during the decomposition and death of the natural life are identical with the Hermetic Separation; entry is by the narrow gate.

quotes.text: can enter in through the narrow gate, as in the Mysteries we have already described
when the great ordeals are passed through during the decomposition and death of the natural life

ambiguities.quote: in order to discover this Reason
readings: 'this Reason' refers back to the Light of ¶11.
It refers to the reason to which the subordinate powers were adapted in ¶11, or to a Reason introduced before this chunk.
ambiguities.basis: ¶11 ends with 'adaptation of the subordinate powers to reason' and 'substant light'; ¶21 later says of the Reason 'For it is Light indeed'.

ambiguities.quote: But the contemplation which absolves the Second part of our admonition is celestial
readings: The first part is Basil's preceding advice to search with eyes and hand (experience); the second is spiritual contemplation.
It refers to a division in Basil's text not reproduced here.
ambiguities.basis: ¶13 earlier quotes Basil on 'thine own eyes and hand'; but n14 ('Disce igitur, etc.') and n15 ('Chariot of Antimony') are different citations.

ambiguities.quote: triply imprisoned in the dark body’s hold
readings: A rhetorical intensive: deeply imprisoned.
Three specific enclosures, possibly related to the three menstruals of ¶14; the chunk does not say so.
ambiguities.basis: No gloss of 'triply' in ¶13; ¶14 mentions 'many links' and three menstruals.

ambiguities.quote: by rotting the moles of the body (i.e., of the ethereal body)
readings: The parenthetical glosses are Eirenaeus' own words.
They are Atwood's insertions redirecting the reading to an 'ethereal body'.
ambiguities.basis: The parentheticals '(i.e., of the ethereal body)' and '(of the same body)' sit inside an attributed quotation and are not marked as editorial.

ambiguities.quote: Take counsel; be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire
readings: Continuation of the Eirenaeus quotation.
Atwood's own added counsel.
ambiguities.basis: No quotation marks; footnote (16) closes the whole paragraph (supports reading 1); the shift to 'Take counsel' and 'your' could mark a new speaker.

ambiguities.quote: Seek it in the house of Aries, and draw it from the depths of Saturn; let Mercury be the internal, and your signal the Doves of Diana
readings: Literal astrological or chemical directions for where to find the internal Fire and what sign to watch.
Veiled names for inner conditions or stages of the work.
ambiguities.basis: ¶14 gives no gloss; 'it' follows 'your internal Fire', and the preceding contrast with the Athanor's fire favours an inward reference, but the specific names are unexplained.

readings: The imprisoned fire / seed of gold of ¶14.
The 'flower of human intellect' of ¶13.
ambiguities.basis: ¶15 'On some such errand' links it to the preceding search without naming the referent.

ambiguities.quote: that which he shall bear away from thence, Centaur-like, in both his Hands
readings: 'Both his Hands' renders the Latin 'Ambabus valet hic minibus sibi sumere' (¶18): he carries away much.
'Centaur-like' implies a double, man-and-beast nature in the bearer; unexplained.
ambiguities.basis: ¶18 Latin has 'Ambabus'; 'Centaur-like' is Atwood's addition and is not glossed.

ambiguities.quote: such a Mercury as is bottomless, or whose center it can never find, but by discovering its own
readings: 'it' is the gold-body, which reaches the Mercury's center only by discovering its own center (self-discovery).
'it' is the Mercury, which never finds its center except by self-discovery.
'bottomless' simply means unfathomable or inexhaustible.
ambiguities.basis: The grammar of ¶19 permits either referent; the sentence's subject is the gold thrown into Mercury. ¶13's 'self-knowledge' of the spiritual intellect lends some support to reading 1.

ambiguities.quote: Salt is good, but if the Salt have lost its savor wherewith shall it be seasoned?
readings: Natural intellect, lacking penetrative essence, cannot season or transform the Spirit; a higher Intellect is needed.
A warning that if the agent itself is corrupted, nothing can restore the work.
ambiguities.basis: It follows directly on 'neither is its essence so acutely penetrative as to operate the change required' (¶20); no gloss.

translations.translation: shut away, it sits farther off (the book continues: 'it is far off, gotten in the penetralia')

translations.original: Alte vestiga oculis: et rite repertum, Carpe manu; namque Ipse volens facilisaque sequetur, Si te fate vocant; aliter, non viribus ullis Vincere, nec duro poteris convellere ferro
translations.translation: Search on high with your eyes, and when it is duly found, pluck it with your hand; for of itself it will follow, willing and easy, if the fates call you; otherwise you will not be able to overcome it by any strength, nor tear it away with hard iron.

translations.original: At quaecunque virum ducit prudnetia cordis Mercurii ingedier spuluncam plurima ubi ille Deponit bona, stat quorum praegrandis acervus Ambabus valet hic minibus sibi sumere, et ista Ferre domum, valet hic vistare incommoda cuncta.
translations.translation: But whatever man prudence of heart leads to enter the cave of Mercury, where he lays down very many goods, of which a very great heap stands, this man can take them for himself with both hands and carry them home; this man can avoid all troubles. (¶19 gives Atwood's interpretive paraphrase, not a translation.)

translations.original: Nescit Sol comitis non memor esse sui
translations.translation: The Sun knows not how to be unmindful of its companion.

translations.original: Ignire ignis amat, non aurificare sed, aurum.
translations.translation: Fire loves fire, say they, not to make gold, but to assimilate it.

translations.original: Intellectus naturam habens subtilem ad intelligendum res intelligibles, participat, cum entibus intensis et cum entibus extensis, viz., cum intenso calore corporis, cum quo conjunctus est et cum intense bonitate sustentata in suis intensis concretis
translations.translation: Intellect, having a subtle nature for understanding intelligible things, participates with intensive beings and with extensive beings, namely with the intense heat of the body with which it is joined, and with the intense goodness sustained in its intense concretes.

threads.note: 'this Light' refers back to a Light discussed before this chunk.
'this Reason' refers back to a Reason introduced before this chunk (or to ¶11; see ambiguities).
Lully, Michael Maier and others: 'to which in the Practice we shall have occasion to allude' (forward to the Practice).
Entry 'through the narrow gate, as in the Mysteries we have already described' (back to the earlier account of the Mysteries).
Atwood says it 'will be necessary... to discuss the point' and to 'substantialize without deforming this Intellectual Science' (forward).
'in a former citation from his book to the Athenians, Paracelsus saying, that Separation is the greatest miracle' (back to an earlier citation).
Separation 'identical with that which is described as taking place in the Mysteries' during 'the great ordeals' (back to the Mysteries chapters).
'as before shown, no foreign admixture is allowed to enter' (back to an earlier demonstration).
